extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, publishers, and readers interested in publication integrity and retractions
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging whether a submitted or published research article meets norms of originality, scientific validity, peer-review scrutiny, and contribution to its field. Includes publisher-side screening and investigation practices that lead to retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality / No substantial overlap
rubrics_metrics.description: The work should not substantially overlap with previously published material; substantial overlap is grounds for concern and can trigger retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals expect submissions to be original and not duplicate substantial material. If an investigation concludes that a paper "substantially overlapped with another paper," retraction is an appropriate course of action. Note: detection tools can miss overlap depending on timing of publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific validity / Coherent, sensible content
rubrics_metrics.description: The article's content must be scientifically valid and not contain nonsensical material; presence of nonsensical content undermines confidence in the research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors cited "concerns regarding the originality and scientific validity" and specifically raised "nonsensical content" as a reason to retract. Nonsensical or gobbledygook material is a substantive defect that can justify loss of editorial confidence and retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review should detect substantive problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer reviewers and editors are expected to identify serious problems (e.g., nonsense, poor methodology, duplication) before publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that the nonsense and duplication "could easily have been detected with some peer review." While the specific peer review process for the case wasn't disclosed, the expectation is that peer review acts as a gatekeeper to catch obvious defects prior to publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism screening / use of detection tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers should run plagiarism checks on submissions to detect duplicated text or content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The journal asserted it runs plagiarism checks on all submissions. However, the effectiveness of such tools can be reduced if an overlapping work is published after the submission date, so screening is not foolproof and depends on timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to submission policies regarding duplicate material
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must follow submission policies that prohibit duplicated material and self-plagiarism; violation may lead to retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The publisher pointed to its submission policies outlining expectations for authors regarding duplicated material; given an investigation finding substantial overlap, retraction was deemed appropriate under those policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial investigation and governance processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns raised about a paper should trigger an investigation following established editorial processes, including consulting editorial board experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The journal described investigating concerns carefully, following established processes and seeking expert advice from the Editorial Board. Such processes determine whether to correct, retract, or take other actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility / Availability of code and data
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing code/data is a practical expectation for validating computational or numerical results; withholding them weakens credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters invoked a strict validation norm summarized as "release the code or never happened," indicating community expectations that results, especially numerical simulations, should be reproducible and open for scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance and contribution to the field
rubrics_metrics.description: A submission should meaningfully contribute to the advancement of the targeted discipline rather than being merely whimsical or metaphorical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article quotes researchers saying that romantic-relationship modeling papers are often "whimsical and metaphorical" and "have not contributed much to the advance of social psychology." Difficulty in validating models (e.g., fictional relationship models) counts against their scientific value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundary of what counts as 'science' (empirical grounding)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be treated as scientific research, studies should involve studying the real world or offer empirical grounding rather than purely fictional constructs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A former editor's policy was mentioned: defining "science" as needing to involve studying the real world to avoid accepting purely fictional or non-empirical modeling as scientific contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of multiple simultaneous/substantially similar submissions (self-plagiarism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should not submit substantially similar manuscripts to multiple journals or republish the same material across papers (self-plagiarism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments suggested the case may involve self-plagiarizing where an author submitted similar papers to different journals at similar times, resulting in duplicated paragraphs across submissions — a practice that can lead to retraction when discovered.
